cues.text: Now let's move through the mobile generations.
One G carried analogue voice.
Two G introduced digital voice and SMS.
Three G brought mobile data, while four G, or LTE, provides all-IP broadband.
Five G uses New Radio and a five G core for flexible service classes.
The radio access network connects user equipment to base stations, called g N B in five G.
Transport connects these to the core, which manages mobility, sessions, authentication and routing.
Standalone five G uses the five G core; non-standalone deployments can rely on an LTE anchor, affecting available features.
Massive MIMO, beamforming, flexible spectrum and denser deployments improve coverage or capacity under suitable conditions.
The table in your notes distinguishes three objectives.
Enhanced mobile broadband, or e M B B, supports high-rate video and broadband.
Ultra-reliable low-latency communication, or U R L L C, targets time-sensitive industrial applications.
Massive machine-type communication, or m M T C, serves large populations of Internet of Things sensors.
These are service objectives, not promises that every five G deployment achieves a particular speed or delay.
Network slicing creates logical, service-oriented networks on shared infrastructure, separating resources and policies; real isolation and service-level agreements still need engineering.
Lower frequency bands generally help coverage, mid-bands balance capacity and coverage, and millimetre-wave or high bands provide capacity at shorter range with obstacles affecting propagation.
Costs, spectrum, backhaul, power, device support, security and coverage all constrain deployment.
Six G remains a research and standardisation vision in these notes.
Potential techniques include higher frequencies, AI-native optimisation, integrated sensing and communications, and non-terrestrial connectivity.
Do not confuse research targets with universal deployed performance.
